# autopilot_app (Resource)

An app: a unit of consent. It owns repositories, names the senders it accepts work from with the kinds of task it accepts from each, and names the people who may start work for it themselves, with their GitHub logins.

AutoPilot takes a sender's task only when the app the task is billed to, and the app that owns each repository the task touches, accept that sender for that kind. An app may accept a sender that doesn't exist yet, so the app and the sender can be applied in either order.

Every argument but `name` is optional and sent only when set. Removing one from the configuration empties it at AutoPilot: an app without `accepts` accepts no sender. Narrowing or deleting an app takes effect at once: AutoPilot stops the queued and running tasks the app no longer accepts.

A repository belongs to the first app that claims it. AutoPilot can't tell which app should own one, so review an app's `repos` as you would its access.

`credential` and `when_seats_full` are the app's credential policy: what the model calls of the tasks billed to it run on. A change to either sends both.

`worker_image`, `worker_cpu` and `worker_memory` choose the worker the tasks billed to the app run in: its image, and the size of the AWS Fargate task it runs as. `worker_cpu` and `worker_memory` are one size, set together, and a change to either sends both.

`auto_review` has AutoPilot review the app's pull requests on its own, with no label, as the app's own service identity, and lets the GitHub Actions workflows it lists ask for those reviews. It is one setting, and a change to any of its fields sends all of them.

`review_also_reads` lets the reviews of the app's repositories read other repositories of the same owner, read-only. Anyone who can push a branch to one of the app's repositories, and anyone who can read its reviews, can see what those repositories hold.

`work_item_projects` lets the reviews of the app's repositories read the work items a pull request names, from the listed projects of the work tracker AutoPilot reads. Anyone who can push a branch to one of the app's repositories can have a review read any item of those projects, and anyone who can read its reviews can learn what such an item asks.

`max_reviews_per_day` is the daily cap on the reviews people ask for from GitHub on each of the app's repositories.

`approve_as_user` lets the app's reviews approve, as a separate GitHub user that is a code owner, on a repository where AutoPilot otherwise only comments.

An app with this name that already exists is not taken over, even when its values match: the create fails and says to import it. The one exception is a create whose earlier attempt went unanswered (a gateway's 502, say) before an identical app answered: that attempt may have made the app, and the provider can't tell, so it takes the app as its own. `create_before_destroy` doesn't fit an app: the name is its key.

Import by name: `terraform import autopilot_app.billing billing`.

## Example Usage

```terraform
locals {
  developers = ["first.developer@example.com", "second.developer@example.com"]
}

resource "autopilot_app" "billing" {
  name = "billing"

  # The repositories this app owns. A repository belongs to one app at most.
  repos = ["example-org/billing-api", "example-org/billing-web"]

  # The senders it accepts work from, and the kinds it accepts from each.
  accepts = [
    {
      sender = "tracker"
      kinds  = ["implement-work-item", "fix-error", "review-pr"]
      # Let the tracker's review-pr tasks approve or request changes.
      can_decide = true
      # Let GitHub's auto-merge be turned on for the pull requests the
      # tracker's tasks open, when a task asks for it. GitHub merges each one
      # once the repository allows auto-merge and its required checks and
      # reviews pass.
      can_auto_merge = true
    },
    {
      sender = "monitor"
      kinds  = ["fix-error"]
    },
    {
      # Pull request reviews the developers start from GitHub.
      sender = "autopilot-github"
      kinds  = ["review-pr"]
      # Let them approve or request changes. On a pull request that may be
      # the asker's own they still only comment, unless can_decide_own_pr
      # is set to true as well. That check goes by the pull request's author
      # alone, so read can_decide's caveats before turning this on.
      can_decide = true
      # Approve only pull requests rated low risk. An approval of one rated
      # medium or high, or one it couldn't rate, is posted as a comment
      # instead, saying why. Requests for changes aren't limited.
      approve_up_to = "low"
    },
  ]

  # The people who may start work for this app themselves.
  developers = local.developers

  # Each developer's GitHub login, so a review they start from GitHub runs
  # in their name. Every developer here must be in developers too.
  github_logins = [
    { login = "example-first-dev", developer = "first.developer@example.com" },
    { login = "example-second-dev", developer = "second.developer@example.com" },
  ]

  # What its tasks' model calls run on: a Claude seat when one has room,
  # and Bedrock when every seat is full.
  credential      = "seat_first"
  when_seats_full = "fall_back"

  # The worker its tasks run in: the ruby image, on a bigger task than the
  # default of 2 vCPU and 8 GB.
  worker_image  = "ruby"
  worker_cpu    = 4096
  worker_memory = 16384

  # Review each pull request into the default branch when it is opened or
  # marked ready, with no label, as the app's own service identity. Drafts
  # wait until they are ready, and bots' and forks' pull requests are
  # skipped.
  auto_review = {
    events      = ["opened", "ready_for_review"]
    max_per_day = 50
    # Let them approve pull requests rated low risk. A developer's own pull
    # request still only gets a comment, unless can_decide_own_pr is set to
    # true as well. With it off, they decide only once every developer's
    # GitHub login is in github_logins: until then, any pull request may be
    # a developer's own.
    can_decide    = true
    approve_up_to = "low"
  }

  # Let the reviews of this app's repositories read the work item a pull
  # request names, such as EXAMPLE-123 in its title or branch, from these
  # projects of the work tracker AutoPilot reads, and check the change
  # against what the item asks. Anyone who can push a branch to these
  # repositories and have it reviewed can have any item of these projects
  # read, so list only projects they may read.
  work_item_projects = ["EXAMPLE"]

  # Take up to 50 reviews a day that people ask for from GitHub, with the
  # label or the command, on each of this app's repositories, instead of
  # AutoPilot's default of 20. Automatic reviews don't count against it.
  max_reviews_per_day = 50
}

resource "autopilot_app" "infrastructure" {
  name  = "infrastructure"
  repos = ["example-org/infrastructure"]

  # Review a pull request only when a GitHub Actions workflow asks, such as
  # once the repository's CI passes. The workflow's job has
  # `id-token: write` and asks AutoPilot with the OIDC token GitHub gives
  # it, so no secret is stored. AutoPilot's own documentation has a
  # workflow to copy. Only this file on the main branch may ask: a pull
  # request's own copy of it can't.
  auto_review = {
    # Required with workflows. [] means nothing is reviewed on its own.
    events    = []
    workflows = ["example-org/infrastructure/.github/workflows/autopilot-review.yml@refs/heads/main"]
  }

  # Let the reviews of this app's repositories also read the modules its
  # Terraform roots use, read-only, at the ref each module source pins.
  # Each must have the same owner as one of repos. Anyone who can push a
  # branch to example-org/infrastructure and have it reviewed, and anyone
  # who can read its reviews, can see what these repositories hold.
  review_also_reads = ["example-org/terraform-modules"]

  # Where AutoPilot otherwise only comments on this repository, let a review
  # that may approve (can_decide) post its approval as a separate GitHub user
  # that is a code owner, whose token AutoPilot's service holds. AutoPilot's
  # GitHub App then never approves or requests changes here itself. It does
  # nothing unless the service has that user's token.
  approve_as_user = true
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) The app's name, which is its key and the `billing.app` of the work it pays for: a lowercase letter or digit, then lowercase letters, digits, `_` and `-`, at most 64 characters. Changing it replaces the app: Terraform deletes the old one, which stops its queued and running work at once, then creates the new one.

### Optional

- `accepts` (Attributes Set) The senders this app accepts work from, each at most once, with the kinds of task it accepts from each. At most 20. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--accepts))
- `approve_as_user` (Boolean) Whether this app's reviews may approve on a repository where AutoPilot otherwise only comments, by an approval AutoPilot's service posts as a separate GitHub user that is a code owner there, whose token the service holds, in place of AutoPilot's GitHub App, which can't be a code owner. It does nothing unless the service has that user's token configured, and nothing on any other repository. With both, AutoPilot's GitHub App never approves or requests changes there itself: it posts each review as a comment, an approval goes as that user, and a review that would request changes stays a comment. Only the reviews of the senders built into AutoPilot (`autopilot-mcp` and `autopilot-github`) and automatic reviews use it, and every other rule a deciding review meets still decides whether it approves: `can_decide` (an `accepts` entry's, or `auto_review`'s), `can_decide_own_pr`, `approve_up_to` and the risk rules. An approval from a code owner can meet a branch's required code owner review on its own, so turn this on only where that is acceptable. Off unless set: leaving it out is the same as `false`. Turning it off refuses or stops the reviews there still queued or running that may decide; approvals already posted are still dismissed when someone pushes, while the service holds the token. Turning it on needs an AutoPilot that knows the field; an older one refuses it with a 422. Off, left out or `false`, it is never sent, except as `false` to turn it off. An AutoPilot rolled back past the field ignores it, so those reviews only comment again, and refuses every write that sends it, but keeps it; it also stops watching the approvals already posted, so dismiss them first. Meanwhile the provider reads the app as off, so a configuration that turns it on plans a change on every run and its applies fail: take it out of the configuration until AutoPilot is rolled forward.
- `auto_review` (Attributes) Automatic reviews: AutoPilot reviews each pull request into the default branch of this app's repositories on its own, with no label or comment, when it is opened, marked ready or pushed to, as `events` says, or when a GitHub Actions workflow listed in `workflows` asks. It reviews only a person's pull request, never a bot's (Dependabot's, or any account GitHub calls a bot), and never a draft until it is marked ready. It reviews only a pull request from a branch of the repository itself, never a fork's, so no one outside the repository can have code run with no person asking; a developer's `autopilot-review` label still reviews a fork's pull request, only as a comment. The review runs as the app's own service identity, `auto-review:<name>`, never a person: that identity asks for it, the app pays, its limits count it, and the review's footer, its check run (`AutoPilot review (automatic)`) and AutoPilot's logs name it. It posts no other comment. Setting this is the app's consent; it needs no `accepts` entry and no developer, and an `accepts` entry for `autopilot-github` doesn't turn it on. A head and base gets one review from GitHub, so a later `autopilot-review` label on the same head gets the automatic review, even one that only commented. Automatic reviews count only against `max_per_day`, never against a repository's daily cap on the reviews people ask for, so they never get a developer's label refused, though they share AutoPilot's one running review from GitHub with labels. Left out, the app has no automatic reviews, and removing it from the configuration turns them off, which also stops the ones queued or running; so does taking `can_decide` or `can_decide_own_pr` away, while fewer `events`, fewer `workflows` or a lower `max_per_day` reach only what comes after. It needs an AutoPilot that knows the field; an older one refuses it with a 422. An AutoPilot rolled back past the field ignores a stored setting and refuses every write that sends one, but keeps it, so it is on again once AutoPilot is rolled forward, even if it was taken out of the configuration meanwhile (Terraform reads it as none, so sends nothing): take it off before such a rollback where that matters. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--auto_review))
- `credential` (String) What the model calls of the tasks billed to this app run on: `bedrock` (Amazon Bedrock, billed per token) or `seat_first` (one of the organization's Claude seats, when one has room). Left out, the app has no policy of its own, and AutoPilot's default applies: `bedrock`. AutoPilot uses seats only while its seat mode is on; with it off, every task runs on Bedrock. Removing it from the configuration takes the app's own policy away. The credential is chosen when a task starts, so a change reaches only the tasks that start after it.
- `developers` (Set of String) The people who may start work for this app themselves, through AutoPilot's MCP server, or from GitHub with a login in `github_logins`: their sign-in logins, which are email addresses, written in lowercase ASCII (AutoPilot refuses anything else). At most 100.
- `github_logins` (Attributes Set) The GitHub logins of this app's developers, for pull request reviews started from GitHub: each pairs a GitHub login with one of `developers`, and a review started from GitHub by that login runs in that developer's name. This decides who can start reviews in a developer's name, so review each pair as you would `developers`. Every `developer` here must also be in `developers`, so take someone's logins out in the same change that takes them out of `developers`. A developer may have more than one login, and each login belongs to one developer. At most 100. It also decides which pull requests count as a developer's own, for reviews from the MCP and from GitHub alike (`can_decide_own_pr`): one whose author isn't among a developer's logins here reads as someone else's, unless that developer has no login here at all. So a missing, wrong or stale pair can let a review approve someone's own work: pair every login a developer uses. Keep it up to date when someone renames their GitHub account: the old login no longer matches them, their pull requests under the new login read as someone else's, and someone else may take the old login. Reviews from GitHub also need the app to accept the `autopilot-github` sender for `review-pr`. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--github_logins))
- `max_reviews_per_day` (Number) The most reviews people ask for from GitHub, with the `autopilot-review` label or the review command, on each of this app's repositories in 24 hours, everyone's together: `1` to `200`. Each repository counts on its own: an app with two repositories and `100` takes 100 a day on each. Every such review AutoPilot recorded on the repository counts, whoever asked and whatever came of it. Automatic reviews and those a workflow asks for never count against it (they have `auto_review.max_per_day`), and nor do reviews asked for on AutoPilot's MCP server. Once a repository is at it, the next ask is refused with a reply on the pull request that names this number. It doesn't change each developer's own limits, and reviews from GitHub still run one at a time across AutoPilot, so a higher cap lets more of them wait in line, where one that waits too long lapses. Left out, a repository gets AutoPilot's default, 20, and removing it from the configuration takes the app back to that. A change reaches the asks that come after it. It needs an AutoPilot that knows the field; an older one refuses it with a 422. An AutoPilot rolled back past the field ignores a stored cap, so every repository is back at the default, and refuses every write that sends one, but keeps it. Meanwhile the provider reads the app as setting none, so a configuration that sets it plans a change on every run and its applies fail: take it out of the configuration until AutoPilot is rolled forward.
- `repos` (Set of String) The repositories this app **owns**, as `owner/name`. A repository belongs to at most one app. AutoPilot matches them without regard to case, so no two may differ only in case. At most 50.
- `review_also_reads` (Set of String) Other repositories that the pull request reviews of this app's own repositories also read, read-only, as `owner/name`: such as the Terraform modules repository whose modules this app's roots use, so a review can read a module at the ref a `source` pins. Only the reviews of this app's repositories read them, whoever asked for the review, and only of a pull request from a branch of the repository itself, never a fork's. No other kind of task, and no other app's review, ever does. Each review reads only those of its own repository's owner. Before the review starts, AutoPilot clones each, every branch and tag, with GitHub tokens of their own that can only read them, never the review's own token, and the review reads them as data, never as instructions: their files for agents, such as `AGENTS.md`, don't apply to it. **This app's repositories' writers and the readers of its reviews can see what these repositories hold:** a review runs the pull request's own code, so anyone who can push a branch to one of this app's repositories and have it reviewed can read everything they hold, every branch and tag, and a review, posted on this app's repository, may quote them. List only repositories those people may read, and review this list as you would `repos`. Each must have the same owner as one of `repos`, compared without regard to case, since a review reads only repositories of its own repository's owner, and none may be one of `repos`, which a review already reads. So an app with no `repos` can list none, and a change that takes a repository out of `repos` must take out the ones only its owner allowed. Each is `owner/name`: the owner letters, digits and `-`, at most 39 characters, and the name letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, at most 100, and not dots alone. AutoPilot compares them without regard to case, so no two may differ only in case. At most 5. An AutoPilot that limits which repositories its apps may reach refuses one outside that limit when it is applied. A repository the GitHub App isn't installed on, that GitHub doesn't know, or that is too large or too slow to clone, is left out of that review, which goes on and says so. Left out, reviews read only their own repository, and removing it from the configuration takes every one away. A change reaches each review that starts after it. Listing some needs an AutoPilot that knows the field; an older one refuses it with a 422. Listing none, left out or `[]`, never sends it. An AutoPilot rolled back past the field ignores the stored list, so reviews read only their own repository, and refuses every write that sends it, but keeps it. Meanwhile the provider reads the app as listing none, so a configuration that lists some plans a change on every run and its applies fail: take them out of the configuration until AutoPilot is rolled forward. Then the next plan shows the list AutoPilot kept, and the apply takes it away unless the configuration lists it again.
- `when_seats_full` (String) With `credential = "seat_first"`, what a task does when every seat is full: `wait` until one has room, or `fall_back` to Bedrock. Required with `seat_first`, and only allowed with it.
- `work_item_projects` (Set of String) The projects of the work tracker AutoPilot reads whose work items the pull request reviews of this app's repositories may read, each by its project identifier: a capital letter, then capital letters and digits, at most 10 characters, such as `PROJ`. A review reads an item, and checks the change against what the item asks, only when the pull request names the item's key (such as `PROJ-123`) in its title, its head branch or the line AutoPilot adds to the pull requests it opens; the item's project is listed here; the pull request is from a branch of the repository itself, never a fork's; and the repository is private or internal, never public. A draft item is never read, nor one the work tracker doesn't show AutoPilot, while an item filed from outside, such as through a public form, is read like any other. Only the reviews of this app's repositories read them, and only where AutoPilot is set up to read the work tracker; elsewhere no review reads one, whatever this lists. A review reads an item as data, never as instructions, and never pastes its text, but what it says, posted on the pull request, can tell anyone who reads the repository's pull requests what the item asks. **Anyone who can push a branch to one of this app's repositories and have it reviewed can name any item of a listed project, and have the review read it:** list only projects whose items this app's repositories' writers, and the readers of its reviews, may read, and review this list as you would `repos`. Kept sorted, each once. At most 20. Left out, reviews read no work item, and removing it from the configuration takes every one away. A change reaches each review that starts after it. Listing some needs an AutoPilot that knows the field; an older one refuses it with a 422. Listing none, left out or `[]`, never sends it. An AutoPilot rolled back past the field ignores the stored list, so reviews read no work item, and refuses every write that sends it, but keeps it. Meanwhile the provider reads the app as listing none, so a configuration that lists some plans a change on every run and its applies fail: take them out of the configuration until AutoPilot is rolled forward. Then the next plan shows the list AutoPilot kept, and the apply takes it away unless the configuration lists it again.
- `worker_cpu` (Number) The CPU of the AWS Fargate task each of this app's tasks runs in, in CPU units, 1024 to a vCPU: `256`, `512`, `1024`, `2048` or `4096`. Set together with `worker_memory`. Left out with it, a task gets AutoPilot's default size, 2 vCPU and 8 GB, and removing both from the configuration takes the app back to it. A bigger task counts against AutoPilot's limits on running tasks and daily spend like any other. The size is chosen when a task starts, so a change reaches only the tasks that start after it.
- `worker_image` (String) The worker image the tasks billed to this app run in: `node`, `ruby`, `ruby-browser`, `python` or `go`. Each is the same worker with that language's tools; `ruby` has Node too, for Rails assets. Choose the app's main language. `ruby-browser` is an opt-in image for Rails system tests: the `ruby` image with Chromium and ChromeDriver, about 500 MB bigger, so choose it only for an app whose tests drive a browser. It needs an AutoPilot that has that image; an older AutoPilot refuses it with a 422. Left out, the app's tasks run in `node`, and removing it from the configuration takes the app back to `node`. The image is chosen when a task starts, so a change reaches only the tasks that start after it.
- `worker_memory` (Number) The memory of that Fargate task, in MiB, at most 16 GB: one that Fargate allows with `worker_cpu`, which is `512`, `1024` or `2048` with `256`; `1024` to `4096` with `512`; `2048` to `8192` with `1024`; `4096` to `16384` with `2048`; `8192` to `16384` with `4096`; each range in steps of `1024`. Set together with `worker_cpu`.

### Read-Only

- `lock_version` (Number) The record's version, which AutoPilot raises on every change. Sent as `If-Match` on updates and deletes.

<a id="nestedatt--accepts"></a>
### Nested Schema for `accepts`

Required:

- `kinds` (Set of String) The kinds of task accepted from that sender, such as `implement-work-item` or `review-pr`. At least one.
- `sender` (String) The sender's name. It need not exist yet.

Optional:

- `approve_up_to` (String) With `can_decide`, the most risk a pull request may carry for that sender's reviews to approve it: `low`, `medium` or `high`. Every review states its pull request's risk. The agent rates it from reading the pull request, and AutoPilot then applies rules of its own that never ask the model and can only raise the rating. For example, a change to CI workflows or to the instructions agents read, or a large diff, is never `low`, and a repository can name its own never-low paths in an `autopilot-never-low-paths` block on its base branch (AutoPilot's admin API documentation lists the rules). An approval rated above this is posted as a comment, with its findings and its level, saying why. So is one whose rating AutoPilot couldn't read, or whose rules it couldn't check, whatever the ceiling, `high` included. A request for changes isn't limited by it. Only with `can_decide = true`, for any sender whose reviews may decide. Left out, every level may be approved, as with `can_decide` alone. The rating is the model's judgment, held up by those rules: a change outside them that a pull request talks its review into rating `low` can still be approved under `low`. AutoPilot asks for the ceiling just before each approval, so a change reaches reviews already running. An AutoPilot release older than this field ignores a stored ceiling and refuses a write that sends one, so if AutoPilot is ever rolled back that far, its reviews approve at any level until it is rolled forward: take `can_decide` off first where a ceiling matters.
- `can_auto_merge` (Boolean) Whether GitHub's auto-merge may be turned on for the pull requests that sender's `implement-work-item` and `fix-error` tasks open on this app's repositories, when the task asks for it. AutoPilot never merges: GitHub merges each pull request once the repository's own settings and ruleset allow it, which means the repository allows auto-merge and its required checks and reviews pass. Off, a person merges. Only with `implement-work-item` or `fix-error` in `kinds`. Off unless set: leaving it out is the same as `false`. Turning it off, or removing the entry or the app, leaves auto-merge on for a pull request that already has it, and GitHub still merges that pull request: turn auto-merge off on the pull request in GitHub.
- `can_decide` (Boolean) Whether that sender's `review-pr` tasks may approve or request changes on this app's repositories, which can count as a required review. Only with `review-pr` in `kinds`. For `autopilot-mcp` and `autopilot-github`, whose reviews run for the person who asked, a review of a pull request that may be that person's own only comments, unless `can_decide_own_pr` is set too. That check goes by the pull request's author alone, so it doesn't stop a developer who pushes their own commits onto someone else's pull request, or a bot's, and then asks: the review may approve their code. GitHub's "require approval of the most recent reviewable push" doesn't stop that either, since AutoPilot isn't the pusher, and GitHub keeps an approval through later pushes unless the branch dismisses stale approvals. On a repository where one approval alone lets a pull request merge, keep that in mind before turning this on. Defaults to `false`.
- `can_decide_own_pr` (Boolean) Whether, with `can_decide`, a review that sender makes for a person may also approve or request changes on a pull request that may be that person's own. Off, such a review only comments. Only for `autopilot-mcp` and `autopilot-github`, whose reviews run for a person (the one who asked on AutoPilot's MCP server, or the developer who asked on GitHub, with the label or the command), and only with `can_decide = true`. A pull request may be the asker's own when its author is a GitHub login that `github_logins` pairs with them, compared without regard to case, or when AutoPilot can't tell: GitHub names no author, or `github_logins` pairs no login with them. So with this off, a review decides only for an asker who has a login in `github_logins`, and only on a pull request whose author isn't one of their logins there. An author no login is paired with reads as someone else's, even when it is another account of the asker's, so pair every login a developer uses. It goes by the author alone, which leaves open what `can_decide` describes: commits pushed onto someone else's pull request. Turning it on lets a developer get an approval of their own pull request that can count as a required review, so set it only where that is acceptable. Off unless set: leaving it out is the same as `false`. When it is turned off, a deciding review of what may be the asker's own pull request that is still queued or running is refused or stopped; ask for the review again.


<a id="nestedatt--auto_review"></a>
### Nested Schema for `auto_review`

Optional:

- `approve_up_to` (String) With `can_decide = true`, the most risk a pull request may carry for an automatic review to approve it: `low`, `medium` or `high`, rated as for `accepts`' `approve_up_to`. An approval rated above it is posted as a comment. Left out, every level may be approved.
- `can_decide` (Boolean) Whether automatic reviews may approve or request changes, which can count as a required review. Independent of any `accepts` entry's `can_decide`, `autopilot-github`'s included. A review decides only on a pull request into the default branch, and requests changes for any finding it marks Important. Defaults to `false`.
- `can_decide_own_pr` (Boolean) Whether, with `can_decide = true`, an automatic review may also decide on a pull request that may be one of this app's developers' own. Off, such a review only comments. A pull request may be a developer's when its author is a GitHub login that `github_logins` pairs with any developer, compared without regard to case, or when AutoPilot can't tell: GitHub names no author, or one of `developers` has no login in `github_logins`, and so could be any author. So with this off, automatic reviews decide only once every developer's GitHub login is paired, and only on a pull request whose author isn't one of those logins. It goes by the author alone, which leaves open what `accepts`' `can_decide` describes: commits pushed onto someone else's pull request. Turning it on lets a developer's own pull request get an approval no other person gave, which can count as a required review: set it only where that is acceptable. Defaults to `false`.
- `events` (Set of String) The pull request actions that start an automatic review on its own: `opened`, `ready_for_review` (a draft marked ready) and `synchronize` (each push to it). Defaults to `opened` and `ready_for_review`. With `synchronize`, every push is a new head and so a new review, within `max_per_day`. At least one, unless `workflows` lists one: `[]` with `workflows` means only those workflows ask, and AutoPilot reviews nothing on its own. With `workflows` listed it must be set, even to the default, so the configuration says on purpose whether pull requests are also reviewed when they open.
- `max_per_day` (Number) The most automatic reviews of this app's repositories in 24 hours, every one AutoPilot recorded counting, however it ended: `1` to `200`. Defaults to `50`. It is their only daily cap: they don't count against a repository's cap on the reviews people ask for (`max_reviews_per_day`), and those don't count against it. Each runs only on one of the organization's Claude seats, one review from GitHub at a time.
- `workflows` (Set of String) The GitHub Actions workflows that may ask for one of this app's automatic reviews, for a repository that wants a review when no event can say, such as once its CI passes. A job of a listed workflow asks AutoPilot with the OIDC token GitHub gives a job that has `id-token: write`, so no secret is stored anywhere. AutoPilot's own documentation on reviews a workflow asks for has a workflow to copy and the checks it makes on each ask. Each entry is the workflow as GitHub names it in that token (`job_workflow_ref`): `owner/repo/.github/workflows/<file>.yml@refs/heads/<branch>` (or `.yaml`), such as `example-org/billing-api/.github/workflows/autopilot-review.yml@refs/heads/main`. Only a branch: a pull request's ref, a tag or a commit is refused, so a pull request that changes the workflow can't ask with its own copy. `owner` is letters, digits and `-`, at most 39 characters; `repo` is letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, at most 100, and not dots alone; the file is straight in `.github/workflows`, letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, at most 200, then `.yml` or `.yaml`; and the branch is letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `/` and `-`, at most 200, as git allows it: not starting with `.`, `-` or `/`, not ending with `/`, `.` or `.lock`, and with no `..`, `//` or `/.`. AutoPilot compares `owner/repo` without regard to case and the rest exactly, so no two entries may differ only in the case of `owner/repo`. At most 20. Defaults to none. The repository the job runs in must be one this app owns. The workflow file may be in another repository, called as a reusable workflow, and then whoever can push to that branch there decides what asks. An ask is one of this app's automatic reviews in every other way: the same identity, `max_per_day`, deciding knobs and check run, and the same rules on which pull requests get one. With any listed, `events` must be set. It needs an AutoPilot that knows the field; an older one refuses it with a 422, and with `events = []` names `events` in the refusal, since it takes no empty `events`. An AutoPilot rolled back past the field refuses every write that sends it, reads an app that lists workflows and no event as having no automatic reviews, and drops the workflows on any write it takes to the app; the next apply after AutoPilot is rolled forward sends them again. Take them off before such a rollback where that matters.


<a id="nestedatt--github_logins"></a>
### Nested Schema for `github_logins`

Required:

- `developer` (String) The developer that login belongs to: their sign-in login, an email address in lowercase ASCII, as it is written in `developers`.
- `login` (String) A GitHub login, written in lowercase (AutoPilot refuses uppercase): a letter or digit, then letters, digits, `-` and `_`, at most 39 characters.

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
# Import an app by its name.
terraform import autopilot_app.billing billing
```
